structure.title: I
structure.summary: The chapter opens with Nick Carraway, Nick Carraway, reflecting on his father's advice to reserve judgment due to unequal life advantages, a principle that made him a confidant in college but left him disillusioned after returning from the East, except for Jay Gatsby, whom he uniquely admires for his extraordinary hope. In the spring of 1922, Nick moves alone to West Egg, renting a modest eighty-dollar bungalow next to Gatsby's lavish mansion; after initial loneliness, he feels settled when a stranger asks him for directions to West Egg village. He begins studying finance with twelve new books on banking and investment, symbolizing his ambition to become a 'well-rounded man.' On a warm evening, he drives to East Egg to visit his cousin Daisy Buchanan and her husband Tom, whom he knew at Yale; they host him in their grand Georgian Colonial mansion, where Daisy’s captivating voice and Tom’s aggressive demeanor create an atmosphere of fragile elegance. During dinner, Tom espouses racist theories from The Rise of the Coloured Empires, a telephone call from his mistress in New York is ignored by Daisy and Jordan Baker, and Daisy confides to Nick that she hopes her daughter will be a 'beautiful little fool.' After dinner, Nick leaves in his car, having been told by Daisy he is rumored to be engaged out West—a claim he denies—and as he stands alone in his yard, he sees Gatsby standing on the lawn, arms outstretched toward a distant green light at the end of a dock, before vanishing into the night.

structure.title: II
structure.summary: On a summer afternoon, Nick Carraway travels by train with Tom Buchanan from West Egg to New York, stopping at the desolate Valley of Ashes where Tom forcibly pulls Nick off to meet Myrtle Wilson at her husband George B. Wilson’s run-down garage. They take a taxi to New York, where Myrtle buys an Airedale puppy, cold cream, and magazines before arriving at a small, overcrowded apartment on 158th Street. Tom retrieves whisky from a locked bureau, and Myrtle calls her sister Catherine and the McKees, who arrive and join the gathering; Myrtle changes into a cream chiffon dress and adopts an artificially haughty demeanor as the party grows increasingly raucous with alcohol, superficial chatter, and strained social posturing. The tension erupts when Myrtle repeatedly shouts Daisy’s name, provoking Tom to brutally break her nose, leading to chaos—women scramble to help her, blood stains the bathroom floor, and she tries to hide her injury with a copy of Town Tattle; Chester McKee awakens, stares at the scene, then leaves without speaking, later inviting Nick to lunch. Overwhelmed, Nick exits the apartment and ends up alone in the cold, dim interior of Pennsylvania Station, reading the Tribune and waiting for the four o’clock train.

structure.title: III
characters_present: The unconscious passenger in the coupé
structure.summary: The chapter opens with Nick Carraway, Nick, receiving a formal invitation to attend one of Jay Gatsby’s extravagant Saturday evening parties at his Long Island mansion, where guests arrive by Rolls-Royce, station wagon, and motorboats, dancing under colored lights and drinking champagne amid orchestral music. Amid wild rumors—Gatsby is a murderer, a German spy, or an Oxford man—Nick wanders the chaotic scene, meeting Jordan Baker, Lucille, and an owl-eyed man astonished by Gatsby’s unread, real books with uncut pages, yet remains one of the few who has not met the host until Gatsby himself reveals his identity beside Nick at a table, casually mentioning their shared wartime service in France and inviting him to fly in his hydroplane the next morning. As the party descends into disorder—with drunken women weeping, couples fighting, and Owl Eyes crashing Gatsby’s new coupé into a wall—Gatsby remains sober and detached, observing from afar before standing alone on the porch to bid farewell as the moon shines over the empty estate, while Nick later reflects on his lonely New York routine, his growing but uneasy connection with Jordan Baker, her dishonesty about damaging a borrowed car and cheating in a golf tournament, and his unresolved emotional ties to a woman back home to whom he still writes letters signed 'Love, Nick'.

structure.title: IV
structure.summary: On a Sunday morning in West Egg, Gatsby’s mansion erupts into chaotic revelry as dozens of guests—among them Chester Beckers, Snell, Klipspringer, Edgar Beaver, and Henry L. Palmetto—arrive by car from East Egg, West Egg, and New York, indulging in lavish excess while knowing nothing of their host; later, on a late July morning, Gatsby picks up Nick Carraway in his cream-colored car with nickel accents and delivers an intense, fabricated biography claiming Oxford education, aristocratic European life, and war honors from Montenegro, producing a medal and photograph as proof, while evading a police stop with a white card; at noon in a cellar restaurant on Forty-second Street, Gatsby introduces Nick Carraway to Meyer Wolfshiem, a grotesque man with hair growing from his nostrils and cuff buttons made of human molars, who recounts the murder of Rosy Rosenthal before Gatsby abruptly excuses himself to make a phone call and vanishes upon seeing Tom Buchanan; meanwhile, Jordan Baker recalls an October day in 1917 when she saw Daisy Fay in her white roadster with Lieutenant Jay Gatsby in Louisville, later revealing Daisy’s tumultuous engagement and marriage to Tom Buchanan, including her drunken breakdown the night before her wedding over a $350,000 pearl necklace, and how, six weeks prior, she recognized Gatsby’s name as the same officer from that long-ago encounter; finally, at twilight in Central Park, Jordan reveals Gatsby bought his mansion solely so Daisy could see the green light across the bay, and he has spent five years waiting for Nick Carraway to invite her to tea so he can reunite with her without appearing desperate, a modest request that shocks Nick Carraway, who then turns his attention to Jordan, drawn to her by the haunting phrase: 'There are only the pursued, the pursuing, the busy, and the tired.'

structure.title: V
structure.summary: On a rainy night in West Egg, Nick returns home to find Gatsby’s mansion brilliantly lit but empty, with only wind causing the lights to flicker; Gatsby approaches him awkwardly, suggesting a late-night trip to Coney Island or a swim, then nervously probes Nick about his income and offers a side business opportunity, which Nick declines. The next morning, Nick invites Daisy to tea, warning her not to bring Tom, and as heavy rain pours, Gatsby sends a man to cut Nick’s grass and delivers a greenhouse full of flowers. Gatsby arrives in a white flannel suit, silver shirt, and gold tie, visibly shaken, obsessing over the tea setup and weather; when Daisy arrives by large open car, Gatsby nearly knocks over a mantelpiece clock in his emotional distress, and the two reunite in tearful silence before gradually relaxing, Gatsby radiating joy as he invites her to tour his mansion. They walk through the estate’s gardens—admiring jonquils, hawthorn, plum blossoms, and kiss-me-at-the-gate—entering through the postern gate into an eerily silent house filled with opulent rooms like Marie Antoinette music-rooms and Restoration Salons, passing Mr. Klipspringer in pajamas doing liver exercises. In Gatsby’s study, he serves Chartreuse and dramatically unveils his collection of shirts, throwing dozens onto the table in cascades of silk, linen, and flannel adorned with stripes, plaids, and monograms, which overwhelms Daisy into uncontrollable sobs. As the rain clears, Gatsby points out the green light on Daisy’s dock, its symbolic power diminished; he shows her photographs of Dan Cody and a youthful portrait of himself in yachting gear, along with newspaper clippings about her, while a phone call about a misplaced guest from Detroit interrupts their intimacy. Pink and golden clouds appear over the Sound, inspiring Daisy to softly wish to enclose Gatsby within them, and after Klipspringer reluctantly plays piano songs like 'The Love Nest' and 'One thing’s sure and nothing’s surer', Nick departs alone into the rain, leaving Gatsby and Daisy lost in each other, emotionally reconnected, with Gatsby holding Daisy’s hand as she speaks softly to him.

structure.title: VI
structure.summary: A New York reporter arrives at Gatsby’s mansion seeking a statement, drawn by growing rumors of Gatsby’s mysterious past—legends including an underground pipeline to Canada and a secret boat-house—confirming his near-celebrity status. The narrative then reflects on Gatsby’s origins as James Gatz of North Dakota, who, at seventeen, rowed out to Dan Cody’s yacht anchored in Little Girl Bay on Lake Superior, adopted the name Jay Gatsby, and spent five years working aboard the Tuolomee in multiple roles while traveling three times around the continent; during this time, he learned to avoid alcohol after witnessing Cody’s drunken excesses, but was later cheated out of his $25,000 inheritance by Ella Kaye after Cody’s death, leaving him with only the refined identity he had forged. Weeks later, Nick Carraway visits Gatsby’s mansion on a Sunday afternoon and is startled to find Tom Buchanan, Mr. Sloane, and a woman in a brown riding-habit arriving on horseback; Gatsby, visibly nervous, insists they stay for drinks and supper, but they subtly exclude him, and when he offers to follow them in his car after admitting he owns no horse, Sloane abruptly departs with the woman, leaving Gatsby stranded. Later that week, Tom and Daisy attend one of Gatsby’s parties, where Daisy is both fascinated and appalled by the extravagance, while Tom grows hostile, dismissing guests as bootleggers and parvenus and interrogating Gatsby’s background; Gatsby, desperate to reclaim the past, insists Daisy never truly loved Tom and demands she renounce her marriage—a claim Nick Carraway warns is impossible—and is devastated when Daisy fails to endorse his idealized vision of their rekindled relationship.

structure.title: VII
structure.summary: On a sweltering summer afternoon, Nick Carraway arrives by train at the Buchanans’ house, where he finds Jay Gatsby waiting nervously; tensions erupt as Daisy openly kisses Gatsby and declares her love, prompting Tom to confront Gatsby’s background, ridiculing his Oxford claim and pink suit. The group departs in two cars—Tom insists Gatsby drive his own vehicle while he takes Daisy in the coupé—stopping at Wilson’s garage in the Valley of Ashes, where a sickly George Wilson reveals he plans to flee with Myrtle, unaware Tom is her lover, while Myrtle watches Jordan from the window with jealous terror. At the Plaza Hotel, amid stifling heat, Tom accuses Gatsby of bootlegging through Meyer Wolfsheim’s drugstores; Daisy, overwhelmed, admits she once loved both men but cannot deny her past with Tom, leading Tom to order them to return to Long Island in Gatsby’s car. Later, Myrtle Wilson runs into the road and is struck and killed by a passing yellow car that does not stop; Michaelis witnesses the crash and finds her body mangled, while Tom arrives at the scene and insists his own car is blue, corroborating his alibi with a driver behind them. That night, Nick refuses to enter the Buchanans’ house and waits outside, where Gatsby emerges in his pink suit, confessing Daisy was driving the car and that he will take the blame; Nick observes Tom and Daisy quietly eating together in the kitchen, united in silence, while Gatsby stands alone under the moon, guarding an empty future.

structure.title: VIII
structure.summary: At dawn on Long Island, Nick Carraway rushes to Gatsby’s mansion after hearing a taxi arrive, finding Gatsby despondent after waiting all night for Daisy to appear at her window—she briefly stood there before turning off the light. Inside the vast, dusty house, they search blindly for cigarettes, eventually smoking by the open French windows as Nick Carraway urges Gatsby to flee to Atlantic City or Montreal to avoid suspicion over Daisy’s car, but Gatsby refuses, clinging to the belief that Daisy never truly loved Tom and still chooses him. In a vulnerable recounting, Gatsby reveals his youth as a penniless officer who fell in love with Daisy’s wealth and mystery, took her under false pretenses of social parity, and became irrevocably bound to a dream that vanished when she retreated into her rich life; he later traveled by day-coach to Louisville to walk the streets where they once met, and now, having never used his pool all summer, sits in quiet despair as Nick Carraway prepares to leave for the city. Meanwhile, George Wilson, consumed by grief and convinced the driver of the yellow car murdered Myrtle after finding a new dog-leash on her bureau, fixates on the eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg as divine judgment, and after wandering from Port Roosevelt to Gad’s Hill and then West Egg, asks for Gatsby’s house—knowing his name. At two o’clock, Gatsby dons his bathing suit, instructs the butler to bring any calls to the pool, and carries a pneumatic mattress to the water, alone among yellowing trees; no call comes, and by four o’clock, the chauffeur hears gunshots but does not react immediately. Nick Carraway arrives by car from the station, alarms the household, and together with the butler, gardener, and chauffeur, finds Gatsby’s body floating on the mattress in the pool—moments later, the gardener discovers Wilson’s body in the grass nearby, completing the tragedy.

structure.title: IX
structure.summary: Following Gatsby’s death, Nick Carraway is left alone to manage the chaotic influx of police, photographers, and curious onlookers at Gatsby’s mansion, while media narratives falsely label Wilson a 'madman' and Catherine denies any connection between Myrtle and Gatsby. Despite desperate efforts—calling Daisy, sending a letter via butler to Meyer Wolfshiem, and enduring a mistaken long-distance call from Chicago—Nick Carraway receives no response from those who knew Gatsby. On the third day, Gatsby’s father, Henry C. Gatz, arrives by train from Minnesota, visibly frail and overwhelmed, proudly displaying a tattered childhood book with Gatsby’s self-improvement schedule and a photograph of the mansion; Nick Carraway attempts to notify acquaintances for the funeral, but Klipspringer declines due to a picnic and Wolfshiem refuses, citing avoidance of death-related entanglements. At the funeral in the rain, only Gatz, Nick Carraway, a minister from Flushing, and the servants are present, until the man with owl-eyed glasses, whom Nick Carraway met months earlier in Gatsby’s library, appears unexpectedly, wiping rain from his glasses to view the grave and quietly calling Gatsby 'the poor son-of-a-bitch.' Afterward, Nick Carraway reflects on his Midwestern roots through memories of Christmas train journeys to Chicago, contrasts them with haunting visions of East Egg as an El Greco nightmare, and confronts Jordan Baker, who reveals her engagement to another man; their bitter exchange ends with Nick Carraway admitting he is too old to pretend honor lies in self-deception. In a final encounter on Fifth Avenue, Tom Buchanan admits he told Wilson Gatsby owned the car that killed Myrtle, justifying it as self-defense and framing his own grief over dog biscuits as moral justification, prompting Nick Carraway to conclude that Tom and Daisy are careless people who destroy lives and retreat into wealth. On his last night in West Egg, Nick Carraway walks to Gatsby’s empty house, erases an obscene word scrawled on the steps, and wanders to the beach, reflecting on the vanished natural beauty of the island and Gatsby’s futile pursuit of the green light, culminating in the meditation: 'So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past.'

plot_summary.plot_summary:
In the spring of 1922, Nick Carraway moves from the Midwest to West Egg, Long Island, seeking opportunity in finance and renting a modest home next to the lavish mansion of the mysterious Jay Gatsby. Through his cousin Daisy Buchanan and her husband Tom—wealthy, entitled East Eggers—Nick is drawn into a world of excess and moral decay. He befriends the enigmatic Jordan Baker and is invited to Gatsby’s extravagant parties, where rumors swirl about Gatsby’s past. Gradually, Nick learns that Gatsby’s wealth and spectacle are all orchestrated to win back Daisy, whom he loved five years earlier as a young officer. Gatsby confides in Nick his dream of rekindling their romance, asking him to arrange a quiet meeting; when Daisy visits Gatsby’s home, the emotional reunion seems to reignite their connection, and Gatsby believes he can erase the intervening years and reclaim the past.

As summer intensifies, tensions rise between Gatsby and Tom, who grows suspicious of Gatsby’s origins and wealth. During a heated confrontation at the Plaza Hotel, Daisy admits she once loved both men but cannot renounce her life with Tom, shattering Gatsby’s illusion. That afternoon, Daisy, driving Gatsby’s yellow car, accidentally kills Myrtle Wilson—Tom’s mistress—in the Valley of Ashes. Gatsby resolves to take the blame, clinging to his belief that Daisy will ultimately choose him. Meanwhile, Myrtle’s grieving husband, George Wilson, misled by Tom into believing Gatsby was both Myrtle’s lover and her killer, seeks vengeance. In a tragic culmination, Wilson shoots Gatsby in his pool and then turns the gun on himself, leaving the mansion silent and empty.

In the aftermath, Nick Carraway struggles to organize Gatsby’s funeral, only to find that none of the hundreds who attended his parties care to attend—except for Gatsby’s father, a humble Midwestern man proud of his son’s achievements, and the owl-eyed man from the library, who quietly calls Gatsby 'the poor son-of-a-bitch.' Nick confronts Jordan Baker, who ends their relationship, and later meets Tom, who coldly admits he told Wilson where to find Gatsby, justifying it as protection. Horrified by their carelessness, Nick realizes the East has corrupted its inhabitants, and he returns to the Midwest, haunted by Gatsby’s futile dream of recapturing the past. Standing alone on the beach, he reflects on the green light Gatsby once reached for, and the relentless human struggle against time: 'So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past.'
